newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Aluminium premiums moving upwards.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Aluminium premiums moving upwards.

text.p: Asian aluminium premiums are on an upward tack led by robust demand from Japan's automobile and construction sectors, base metal traders said on Friday.

Premiums in Singapore for western aluminium 20-25 kg ingots were quoted at US$70-85 a tonne, up slightly from last week's $65-$85 level. Premiums for Russian and Indian aluminium 20-25 kg ingots were quoted at about $55 from $50-$55 last week.
Strong U.S. aluminium demand has also spilled over into Asia supporting premiums in the region, the traders said.
Aluminium indications are firm in Singapore, even though premiums for other base metals, over London Metal Exchange cash prices, are languishing around the $20 a tonne level.

"Japanese demand is very strong. The automobile industry is very busy because they're building up their stocks for the summer production season," the aluminium dealer for a Japanese trading house told Reuters.

Earlier this week, Tokyo dealers confirmed that Japanese aluminium premiums for supply contracts in the April-June quarter were set at about $82 a tonne, up $20 from the previous quarter. The South Korean market followed suit with aluminium premiums rising by between $18-$23 a tonne for the same period.
"The Japanese demand is underpinning premiums for the metal (aluminium) here. Demand in the coming months also looks to be good," the general manager of a European metal firm added.
Most of the demand was for Russian and Indian aluminium ingots and dealers fear any shortage will put further upward pressure on premiums.
"The supply for the Russian grade here has dried up. It's beginning to cause something of a squeeze," one trader for a Singapore-based commodity house said.

Aluminium stocks in the LME warehouse in Singapore reached 17,725 tonnes last Tuesday against 22,250 tonnes reported by the LME on February 11. Most dealers expect another fall when the LME stocks report is released later on Friday.
Rumours also swirled among Far East metal dealers that Chinese buyers were back in the aluminium market.
"I understand that the Chinese are picking up some ally (aluminium) supplies and they're back in the market," one said.

"There's bits and pieces, but the Chinese have not aggressively come in yet. In fact, I haven't seen them buying any copper although there's interest in both copper and aluminium," a dealer for a metal trading firm said.
Base metal demand in Southeast Asia, however, remained quiet, traders said.
"Demand here is still no good," a Japanese dealer said. "We have our regular long-term supply contracts, but we can't get any additional spot business at the moment. It is very quiet in the region."

Traders said LME base metal prices appear firm, with nickel supported by continued fears over the possibility that unpaid workers in Russia's huge Norilsk Nickel NKEL.RTS will go on strike in mid-March and disrupt supplies.
"The price of nickel still seems very firm," one trader said, adding "fund buying and the situation in Norilsk is supporting the price."

Metal broker Brandeis said in its daily review that nickel is "still vulnerable to volatile moves either way in the absence of a period of consolidation and a clear near-term direction is unlikely until the market makes a break out of the $7,200-$8,200 range."
Nickel closed on Thursday on the LME at $8,070 a tonne, $20 up on the day but down from a nine-month high of $8,180.
Singapore traders said copper prices on the LME still have some room on the upside, but any move towards $2,400 will be vulnerable to profit-taking.
"It's going to have a difficult time staying above $2,400," a dealer said.
